title: Choose Projects to Grow Your Capital

concept.title: Among the projects you can afford, always take the most profitable one
body: You start with the capital `w` and may finish at most `k` projects, one after the other. Project `i` can be started only if your **current capital is at least `capital[i]`**; when it is finished, your capital grows by `profit[i]` (the capital you needed is not spent). Maximize the capital at the end.

Greedy choice: at each step, among all projects you **can afford now**, take the one with the **largest profit**. Why is it safe? Every project taken adds its profit and can only make **more** projects affordable, so taking the largest profit gives the largest capital after this step and also the largest set of affordable projects among all options that take one project. Capital never decreases, so a project that is affordable now stays affordable.

To do it quickly, sort the projects by the capital they need. A pointer walks through the sorted list and **pushes the profits of all projects that have become affordable** into a **max-heap**; the top of the heap is the best choice.

body.code:
order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: capital[i])
heap, j = [], 0
for _ in range(k):
    while j < n and capital[order[j]] <= w:     # newly affordable projects
        heappush(heap, -profit[order[j]])
        j += 1
    if not heap:
        break                                   # nothing can be afforded: stop
    w += -heappop(heap)                         # take the most profitable one

body: The sort costs O(n log n), and every project enters and leaves the heap at most once. The final capital can reach about 2 * 10^13, so use 64-bit integers.

statement: There are `n` projects. Project `i` needs a capital of at least `capital[i]` to start, and gives a profit of `profit[i]` when finished (the capital needed is not used up). You start with the capital `w` and can finish at most `k` projects, one at a time. Print the largest capital you can have at the end.
inputFormat: The second line has `n` numbers: the profit of each project.
The third line has `n` numbers: the capital that each project needs.

examples.note: With the capital 0 only project 1 (profit 1) can be taken; then the capital is 1, and the project with the profit 3 can be taken: 0 + 1 + 3 = 4.

hints: Sort the projects by the capital they need.
Push the profits of all projects that are affordable into a max-heap.
Take the largest profit, add it to the capital, and repeat up to k times (stop when the heap is empty).

explanation: The projects are sorted by the capital they need; the profits of the affordable ones are pushed into a max-heap, and the largest profit is taken at each of at most k steps.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, k, w = map(int, input().split())
profit = list(map(int, input().split()))
cap = list(map(int, input().split()))

import heapq
order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: cap[i])
heap = []
j = 0
for _ in range(k):
    while j < n and cap[order[j]] <= w:
        heapq.heappush(heap, -profit[order[j]])
        j += 1
    if not heap:
        break
    w += -heapq.heappop(heap)
print(w)
